tasks.task_description: Develop the Goodgrant Foundation's five-year, $100M-per-year investment strategy for US colleges and universities: a prioritized candidate list of schools, the investment amount per school, an estimated return on investment (ROI) appropriate for a charitable organization, and the duration over which the money should be given, all chosen to maximize the likelihood of a strong positive effect on undergraduate student performance while avoiding overlap with the focus of other large grantmakers.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: convert the raw IPEDS/College Scorecard extract into a defendable analytic subset, score every candidate on its demonstrated potential to turn private funding into student outcomes, allocate the $100M by marginal impact per grant dollar, and define a charitable ROI in incremental completions valued at tuition-equivalent plus earnings terms. Assumptions: (A1) the 2,977 schools in the IPEDS UID file are the candidate universe; (A2) a school is evaluable only if it reports both the primary outcome signals - the 150%-time four-year completion rate (C150_4_POOLED_SUPP) and median post-graduation earnings at 10 years (md_earn_wne_p10) - because the expert's practical standard for 'money well spent' is completion plus labor-market value (expert exchange 1); (A3) UGDS >= 100 so reported rates are statistically stable; (A4) the highest populated net-price tier (NPT45 down to NPT41) proxies the per-student annual cost of educating a student; (A5) the grant's effect on completion is a small positive lift with diminishing returns as the grant becomes a larger share of the school's budget - a $100M pool spread over a school is a rounding error against large budgets, so marginal impact favors schools where the grant is material relative to scale but where demonstrated conversion ability exists (expert exchange 2); (A6) the foundation can effectively manage 20-50 schools per year, with 30 as the working point and an average grant near $3.3M per school per year (expert exchange 3); (A7) the five-year horizon matches the foundation's stated five-year program window. Method choice: rank-based composite scoring plus a capped waterfill allocation is sound here because the data contain heavy privacy suppression (about 30% of completion cells), so percentile ranks within the analytic subset are more robust than parametric assumptions, and the cap-waterfill solves the two-sided constraint (grants must be material, but must not dominate a school's budget).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning: 2,977 candidate UNITIDs merged left with the 7,804-row Scorecard file (2,935 matched); 'PrivacySuppressed' text and blanks coerced to NaN in the 18 numeric columns; zero duplicate UNITIDs in either file; 41 candidates unmatched; net-price tiers with negative values (rounding artifacts) clipped at 0. Analytic subset: schools with COST_STU > 0, PCTPELL present, both primary outcomes present, UGDS >= 100 -> 626 schools. Parameters (calibrated inputs): base completion lift dC = 0.03, interval [0.01, 0.05], source: Castleman & Long (2013), NBER WP 19306, https://doi.org/10.3386/w19306 (need-based grant eligibility raises six-year bachelor's completion ~22% relative for students near the cutoff); Denning, Marx & Turner (2019), AEJ: Applied Economics 11(3), https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20180100 (grant eligibility significantly increases degree completion and later earnings; earnings gains recoup grant cost within 10 years); expert exchange 1 (outcome signals are completion and earnings) and exchange 3 (30 schools/yr). Value per completion V = 0.5*COST_STU + 0.25*max(0, md_earn_wne_p10 - 25000) dollars, i.e. half the tuition-equivalent cost of the degree plus a quarter of the earnings premium above the $25k survival floor (gt_25k_p6 anchor). Models: (1) potential score P_i = 0.45*z(comp_i) + 0.30*z(earn_i) - 0.15*z(cost_i) + 0.10*PCTPELL_i, with z-scores computed within the 626-school subset; (2) expected lift dC_i = dC*(0.4 + 1.2*rank(P_i)), capped at 0.10; realized lift dC*_i = dC_i*(1 - exp(-g_i/B_i)) where B_i = UGDS_i*COST_STU_i/1e6 is the budget in $M; (3) marginal completions per grant dollar m_i = UGDS_i*dC_i/B_i; materiality M_i = 1 - exp(-(100/K)/B_i); (4) selection score S_i = 0.45*rank(P_i) + 0.35*rank(m_i) + 0.20*rank(M_i); top K = 30 schools selected; (5) allocation: base grant 100/K = $3.33M to each selected school, remaining budget waterfilled proportionally to m_i, each grant capped at 20% of B_i (expert: grant must be material but not dominant); (6) expected new completions per year N_i = UGDS_i*dC*_i; (7) five-year charitable ROI = sum_i N_i*V_i*5 / $500M. Solution procedure: run code/model.py --K 30 --dC 0.03 --MIN_GRANT 10; sweeps over K in {20,30,50} and dC in {0.01,0.025,0.05} available via --sweep.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: 30 schools selected from 626 evaluable candidates; total allocation exactly $100.0M per year for five years; expected ~272 incremental completions per year (~1,357 over five years); grant sizes range from $1.27M (smallest school, capped at 20% of budget) to $3.66M per school per year, averaging $3.33M. Five-year portfolio ROI = 0.043 in tuition-equivalent terms ($21.5M value of incremental completions per $500M granted), which is conservative: the ProPelled evidence shows grant-funded earnings gains alone recoup the grant cost within ten years, so the true lifetime ROI is several times this figure. Top-5 prioritized list (rank, school, state, enrollment, completion rate, 10-yr median earnings, grant $M/yr, new completions/yr, 5-yr ROI): 1 US Merchant Marine Academy (NY, 958, 0.747, $89k, 1.27, 8.3, 0.127); 2 UConn Stamford (CT, 1224, 0.577, $54k, 2.99, 10.1, 0.045); 3 UConn Avery Point (CT, 645, 0.478, $54k, 1.63, 5.1, 0.042); 4 Massachusetts Maritime Academy (MA, 1362, 0.639, $80k, 3.52, 7.5, 0.052); 5 UConn Tri-Campus (CT, 2382, 0.507, $54k, 3.61, 11.5, 0.044). The full 30-school list with all fields is in results/selected_K30.csv. Interpretation: the portfolio mixes high-completion, low-cost small schools (the maritime academies, VMI) that deliver the most completions per dollar with a handful of larger, affordable public schools (UGA, Clemson, UT Dallas, CUNY Baruch and Queens, Penn State Wilkes-Barre) that add scale and geographic spread; median selected school has a 0.636 completion rate, $52,650 ten-year median earnings, 0.263 Pell share, enrollment 534-26,120. Sensitivity: expected completions scale linearly in dC (458 at dC=0.01, 1,145 at 0.025, 2,290 at 0.05); K=20 slightly raises ROI per dollar but the expert's operational ceiling of 20-50 makes K=30 the right point. Duration: five annual tranches with a mid-program review - the diminishing-returns term in dC*_i makes the strategy self-correcting, and schools whose completion rate does not move after two years should have grants reduced. Limitations and biases: (1) the data are cross-sectional 2015 snapshots, so the model ranks demonstrated status rather than measured causal response to money; the lift parameter bridges that gap but inherits the Texas four-year public context of its sources and may not transfer to small private or for-profit schools; (2) privacy suppression removes the weakest small schools from the analytic subset, so the ranking under-represents genuinely distressed institutions - a deliberate choice given the expert's warning that money at capacity-weak schools may not convert; (3) the net-price tier proxy overstates cost at public schools that serve heavy Pell populations (the true marginal cost is lower); (4) ROI values completions at tuition plus a small earnings premium and omits tax and spillover gains, so it is a floor, not a ceiling; (5) no overlap screening against Gates/Lumina actual 2016 portfolios was possible from the supplied data, so 'not duplicating other large grantmakers' is enforced only indirectly through the mid-sized, affordable-public tilt of the score.
